
# 🌕 The Mid-Autumn Festival (中秋节)
### *Zhōngqiū Jié — a research guide to China's festival of the moon, harvest and reunion*

> 🏮 *"Reunion" is the whole point. For roughly three thousand years, people in China have looked up at the same round moon and thought of the people they love.*

---

The colors and illustrations follow the traditional Chinese palette of the festival: the deep night sky, moon-white, imperial gold and lantern red. The hex values are approximate digital equivalents.

## 🌟 The Festival at a Glance

| | |
|:--|:--|
| **Chinese name** | 中秋节 *Zhōngqiū Jié* ("Mid-Autumn Festival") |
| **Also called** | Moon Festival · Mooncake Festival · Festival of Reunion (团圆节) |
| **Lunar date** | 15th day of the 8th month, when the moon is at its fullest and brightest |
| **Gregorian range** | Anywhere between 7 September and 8 October [4] |
| **In 2026** | **Friday, 25 September** [4]. Mainland China's holiday break runs 25–27 September [33][35]. Hong Kong's day off is the 26th [34]. |
| **Core themes** | Gathering, giving thanks, and praying for good fortune [4] |
| **Status** | Named to China's first national intangible cultural heritage list (20 May 2006) and made a statutory holiday from 1 January 2008 [22] |

> 🌙 **Why this matters:** Modern sources often call it China's second most important traditional festival after Chinese New Year [41]. Its emotional center is family reunion, and the round moon stands for completeness [22][4].

## 📜 History: How a Harvest Rite Became a National Festival

### 🕰️ Timeline

| Era | What was happening |
|:--|:--|
| 🌾 **Shang / Zhou** <br>(c. 1600–256 BCE) | Autumn moon worship as a harvest ritual. CGTN notes that Shang-era inscriptions record moon worship [6], and Wikipedia says autumn full-moon harvest celebrations go back to the Shang [4]. Kings made moon sacrifices in the Western Zhou [1]. A royal system of sun worship in spring and moon worship in autumn is described in Zhou-era rites [2]. The word **"Mid-Autumn"** appears in the *Rites of Zhou*, but only as a marker of season and time, not yet a festival [1]. |
| 🏯 **Han** <br>(202 BCE–220 CE) | Some sources place the earliest written appearance of "Mid-Autumn" in this period. At that point it described harvest time, and the food was porridge rather than mooncakes [2]. Watching the Qiantang River tidal bore around this season is described in Han-era writing [12]. |
| 🎎 **Tang** <br>(618–907) | The festival begins to take shape. Moon-viewing became fashionable among the upper class, with banquets, music and dance, while commoners prayed to the moon for a good harvest. Later, ordinary people joined in [1]. Poets wrote about the moon and the legends of Chang'e were woven in [7]. |
| 🎇 **Song** <br>(960–1279) | The 15th of the 8th month was established as the festival [1]. Celebrations became a city-wide event. In the capital it was a night of feasting, drinking and night markets until dawn, according to Meng Yuanlao's *The Eastern Capital: A Dream of Splendor* [3]. The term "moon cake" appears in the Southern Song [7]. Lantern riddles date from this period [6]. |
| 🐉 **Yuan** <br>(1271–1368) | A popular legend says Han Chinese rebels hid messages in mooncakes to coordinate an uprising against Mongol rule (see [the mooncake section](#-mooncakes-a-closer-look)) [17]. |
| 🏮 **Ming & Qing** <br>(1368–1912) | The festival became one of China's main folk festivals, in some accounts as popular as Chinese New Year [1]. Modern forms of moon offerings and mooncake gifting solidified [3]. Fire-dragon dances and pagoda-burning are listed among the festivities [1]. Lord Rabbit (兔儿爷) worship in Beijing dates from the late Ming [12]. Empress Dowager Cixi reportedly staged elaborate rituals from the 13th to 17th of the eighth month [4]. |
| 📷 **Republican era** <br>(1912–1949) | Photographs show children in Beijing praying to Lord Rabbit [3]. |
| 🇨🇳 **2006–2008** | Listed as national intangible cultural heritage (2006) and made a public holiday (2008) [22][3]. |

### 👑 The emperor's moon

In imperial China, the ruler prayed to Heaven for a prosperous year. The sun was honored on the 15th of the second lunar month, and the moon on the 15th of the eighth. Beijing's **Yuetan Park** was originally the Temple of the Moon, where the emperor offered sacrifices [5].

### 🌅 A note on "how old is it?"

You will often read "over 3,000 years old." That refers to the *moon-worship roots* in the Shang and Zhou periods [2][4]. The festival as most people would recognize it (fixed date, shared customs, poetry, gatherings) took shape in the Tang and was established in the Song [1][8].

## 🐇 Legends of the Moon

The festival's stories are not one canon. Different tellers give different versions.

### 🌙 1. Chang'e Flies to the Moon (嫦娥奔月)

**The most widely told version:**

- Ten suns once scorched the earth. The archer **Hou Yi (后羿)** shot down nine of them and saved humanity [8].
- Hou Yi was rewarded with an **elixir of immortality** (in various tellings from the Queen Mother of the West). He didn't want to become immortal without his wife **Chang'e**, so he asked her to keep it safe [8][9].
- A treacherous apprentice, **Peng Meng**, tried to steal it while Hou Yi was away hunting. To keep it from him, Chang'e swallowed the elixir herself and floated up to the moon [8][9].
- Heartbroken, Hou Yi laid out the fruits and cakes Chang'e loved and made offerings to her. Sympathetic villagers joined in, and this is given as the origin of moon offerings [4][8].

**The darker versions:** (Chang'e has many tales, and the Mid-Autumn origin story is only one of them [37].)

- In one alternate telling recorded in *Handbook of Chinese Mythology*, Hou Yi becomes a tyrant, and Chang'e steals the elixir to *prevent* a cruel king from living forever [4].
- Older accounts, as summarized in a 2026 feature, even cast her as a thief cursed to become a toad [11].

### 🐰 2. The Jade Rabbit (玉兔)

- A rabbit on the moon pounds herbs in a mortar to make the elixir of immortality [10].
- In one popular tale, three immortals disguised as beggars ask a fox, a monkey and a rabbit for food. The rabbit, having nothing to give, offers itself and jumps into the fire, and is rewarded with a place on the moon [51].
- CGTN notes that the rabbit's fertility echoes the lunar cycle, making it a symbol of life and renewal [6].
- Rabbit-on-the-moon myths appear in many cultures, including Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Mesoamerica [10].

### 🌳 3. Wu Gang and the Osmanthus Tree (吴刚伐桂)

A man named Wu Gang wanted to become immortal, made a mistake in heaven, and was banished to the moon. There he must chop a laurel/osmanthus tree that instantly heals itself, so the job never ends [9][3]. The dark shadow you see on the moon is said to be him [52]. Some versions blame laziness [10]. In others, the tree represents the power of regeneration [53].

### 🎶 4. Emperor Xuanzong Visits the Moon Palace

One legend says Tang Emperor Xuanzong (Li Longji) toured the Moon Palace with a Taoist priest and afterward began holding formal celebrations in his palace [9][4].

### 🐇 5. Lord Rabbit (兔儿爷) of Beijing

A Beijing legend says a moon rabbit delivered medicine to every household to protect them from plague. Clay figurines of the rabbit deity, with a human body and a rabbit's head, became a favorite Mid-Autumn toy for children in the Qing dynasty [3][12].

## 🏮 Traditional Customs

### 1. 🌕 Moon Worship (祭月) and Moon Viewing (赏月)

- **How it was done:** Families set a table outdoors under the moon, burned incense, placed mooncakes and fruit as offerings, faced the moon and prayed for good fortune [46].
- **Who:** In several traditions the rite was led by women. Old belief linked the moon with women and rejuvenation, and in some places men did not worship the moon [4]. In the Chaoshan region, women make offerings including cosmetics and perfumes and pray for the family's safety [44].
- **Offerings:** apples, pears, peaches, grapes, pomegranates, melons, oranges and **pomelos**. A clay statue of the Jade Rabbit was traditionally one of the first items bought for the offering table [4].
- **A quiet, elegant custom:** In imperial gardens, families set teacups on stone tables and waited for the moment when the full moon's reflection appeared in the middle of the cup [4].
- **Today:** China Highlights notes that this is fading in big cities but still found in some towns and villages [13].

### 2. 🏮 Lanterns (花灯) and Lantern Riddles (猜灯谜)

- Lanterns in the shape of animals, plants and flowers are carried, hung and displayed [13].
- The link between lanterns and the festival grew from the Tang dynasty [41]. Wikipedia adds that it is difficult to pin down their original purpose, but they were not used with moon worship before the Tang [4].
- **Riddles** written on slips of paper and attached to lanterns have been part of the festival since the Song [6].
- **Regional variations:** In Guangdong, lanterns are tied to bamboo poles and raised near eaves and treetops, a custom called *"shu Zhongqiu"* (树中秋) [29][27]. In Hubei and Hunan, lamps are lit atop stacked-tile "towers" [28]. In Jiangnan, lantern boats float on water [29]. In Guangzhou, children lit "tower lamps" made of broken tiles [12].

### 3. 🥮 Mooncakes (月饼)

Round pastries exchanged as gifts and shared to symbolize completeness and family unity [4]. In some households the eldest person cut a mooncake into pieces and gave one to each family member [4]. Fuller details are in [the mooncake section](#-mooncakes-a-closer-look).

Some imperial extravagances: mooncakes as large as 8 meters in diameter, pressed with designs of Chang'e and the Moon Palace, and stacks of **13 mooncakes** built like a pagoda to represent the 13 months of a full lunisolar year [4].

### 4. 🍶 Osmanthus Wine (桂花酒) and Seasonal Feasting

- Osmanthus blooms at this time of year. **Cassia/osmanthus wine** is the traditional "reunion wine" [4]. It is associated with a harmonious family, wealth and auspiciousness, especially in Zhejiang and Jiangsu [13].
- Historic imperial dishes included **nine-jointed lotus root** (peace) and **watermelon carved into lotus petals** (reunion) [4].
- In Wuxi, people traditionally begin the day with candied taro and osmanthus [28].
- Common seasonal foods include pumpkin, sweet potato, pomelo, walnuts, crab, pork and duck [13]. Lists of Mid-Autumn tables often add hairy crab and osmanthus duck [45].

### 5. 🐉 Fire Dragon Dance (舞火龙)

The most spectacular is Hong Kong's **Tai Hang Fire Dragon Dance**:

- Performed over three nights starting on the 14th of the eighth lunar month. The dragon is woven from pearl grass and studded with thousands of burning incense sticks. Sources vary from about 67 to over 70 meters in length [15][12].
- Hong Kong's tourism board says the dragon carries about **12,000 incense sticks** [14].
- It began in **1880**, after a plague year, and is still run by the Tai Hang Residents' Welfare Association [15]. Villagers believed the incense dragon chased off plague and evil spirits [16].
- It was listed as national intangible cultural heritage in **2011** [15].
- The 2026 performances are listed for **24–26 September** [15].
- At the end, the dragon is traditionally sent off to sea with lanterns, carrying misfortune away [4].

### 6. 🌊 Watching the Qiantang Tidal Bore (观潮)

In Zhejiang, crowds gather along the Qiantang River to watch its famous tidal bore [6]. The custom is described as far back as the Han dynasty [12]. Around the 18th day of the eighth lunar month, the bore near Haining draws crowds from Hangzhou [27]. Yanguan is considered a prime viewing spot [28].

### 7. 🎲 Bo Bing (博饼), the Mooncake Dice Game

A signature custom of southern Fujian (especially **Xiamen**) and Taiwan's Kinmen:

- Players roll **six dice in a ceramic bowl**, and the combination they roll decides which rank of prize they win [25][50].
- Legend credits General Hong Xu, a commander under Zheng Chenggong (Koxinga), who invented the game to lift morale and ease homesickness among troops in Xiamen [24].
- Records of the custom go back to the Ming–Qing period [23]. It is a national-level intangible cultural heritage item [23][25].
- **This year:** Kinmen's county government has organized a Bo-Bing festival for September 2026, including online play [24].

### 8. 🐇 Playing "Lord Rabbit" (玩兔儿爷)

A children's game in Beijing that grew out of the moon-rabbit legend. The clay Lord Rabbit is dressed and displayed, sometimes seated, standing or riding an animal [12][3].

### 9. 💞 Romance and Matchmaking

- The Mid-Autumn moon has long been a favored occasion for weddings and courtship. Girls prayed to Chang'e to fulfill romantic wishes [4].
- In some parts of China, dances were held for young people to meet. In one, a young woman throws her handkerchief into the crowd, and the young man who catches and returns it has a chance at romance [4].

### 10. 🎭 Old Folk Games

Ethnographer Chao Wei-pang recorded games in 1920s–30s Guangdong tied to spirit journeys and fortune-telling: "Ascent to Heaven" (上天堂), "Descent into the Garden" (落花园), and the children's "Encircling the Toad" (围虾蟆), where a child playing the "Toad King" hops around until water is sprinkled on his head [4].

## 🥮 Mooncakes: A Closer Look

![Mooncake illustration](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 📖 Where did they come from?

- **Tang folklore:** One legend says a Turpan merchant offered round cakes to Emperor Taizong after a military victory, and the emperor jokingly invited the moon's toad to enjoy the *hú* (胡) cake [4]. Another version credits Emperor Gaozu [21]. In 1972, a "flower moon cake" from a Tang tomb in Turpan was found, and it is often cited as the earliest physical evidence of such cakes [21].
- **Song:** The term "mooncake" first appears in Southern Song writing, referring at first just to a type of pastry [21][7]. The ties to the festival grew through the Song [4].
- **Yuan–Ming:** The customs of eating and gifting mooncakes flourished, and mooncakes gained the meaning of "reunion" [21].
- **Qing:** Mooncakes became a ubiquitous treat [19].

### 🕵️ The famous "secret message" legend

A widely told story says that in the late Yuan dynasty, Han Chinese rebels, living under restrictions on gatherings and knives, baked slips of paper into mooncakes reading (in paraphrase) that an uprising would take place on the 15th night of the eighth month. The rebellion, led by Zhu Yuanzhang, is said to have contributed to the fall of the Yuan and the rise of the Ming in 1368 [17][4]. Treat this as a **legend** that is widely repeated rather than a firmly documented event. Even a 2026 feature calls it "a widely told legend" [11].

### 🧭 Regional styles

| Style | Home region | Signature traits |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Cantonese (广式)** | Guangdong / Hong Kong | Thin, golden, molded lard-based skin around thick lotus-seed or red-bean paste, often with salted yolk. It became the "default" style partly because Hong Kong exported it heavily from the 1960s [17][20]. |
| **Beijing (京式)** | Beijing / Tianjin | Includes *ti jiang* (提浆), *fan mao* (翻毛) and *zilaihong* (自来红, with a red ring on top). Fillings include nuts, fruits, osmanthus and sugar [19]. Said to have originated in Beijing and Tianjin [42]. |
| **Suzhou (苏式)** | Yangtze Delta | Flaky, multi-layered pastry with both sweet and savory versions, such as fresh pork or shrimp [18][17]. |
| **Yunnan (滇式)** | Yunnan | Xuanwei ham with honey and sugar, sometimes with rose petals [18][11]. |
| **Chaoshan (潮式)** | Eastern Guangdong | Flaky, often large; mung bean, red bean, taro or black-bean-and-potato fillings [42][19]. |
| **Taiwanese** | Taiwan | Traditionally sweet red bean, sometimes with chewy mochi, plus winter melon; many modern versions [43][20]. |

### ✨ The new generation

- **Snow-skin (冰皮月饼):** chilled, unbaked, mochi-like, said to have been invented in Hong Kong [20][11].
- **Ice-cream and jelly mooncakes** [20].
- **Lava custard:** Hong Kong's Maxim's is credited with popularizing flowing-center mooncakes [27].
- **Savory, playful flavors:** including spicy beef [47].
- **Character-shaped and mold-made mooncakes** popular online [30].

### 🔢 Symbolism

- **Round shape:** completeness and reunion [4].
- **Salted duck egg yolk:** represents the moon [20].
- **Standard fillings:** lotus seed paste, red bean paste, taro, and "five kernels" (五仁, a mix of nuts and seeds) [20].
- **Four-piece boxes** are commonly sold as gifts [30]. Even numbers are often considered auspicious, though family customs vary [30].

## 🗺️ Regional & Ethnic Customs

| 📍 Place / group | 🎎 Custom |
|:--|:--|
| **Hong Kong** | Lantern displays around the city, the huge lantern carnival at Victoria Park, riddles, and the Tai Hang Fire Dragon [14]. The day *after* the festival is the public holiday, since celebrations happen at night [4]. |
| **Guangdong** | Offerings to the "Moon Lady" and lanterns on tall bamboo poles [6][29]. |
| **Zhejiang** | Qiantang tidal bore watching [6]. |
| **Fujian (Xiamen)** | Bo Bing dice game [25]. |
| **Beijing** | Lord Rabbit figurines [3]. |
| **Taiwan** | Outdoor barbecues and children wearing hats made from pomelo rind, so that Chang'e will notice them and bestow good fortune [4]. |
| **Chaoshan** | Women-led moon worship with cosmetics offerings [44]. |
| **Dong people (Hunan)** | Women traditionally "steal" vegetables, since the moon goddess is said to shower them with "sweet dew" that brings health and happiness [26]. |
| **Dong people (Guizhou)** | Young men and women meet at agreed places to court [4]. |
| **Zhuang people** | An ancient fable of the Sun and Moon as a couple with stars as their children; the moon is round when pregnant [4]. |
| **Tu people** | "Beating the Moon": a basin of water reflects the moon and is struck with branches [4]. |
| **Maonan people** | "Shooting the Moon": a grapefruit hung on a bamboo pole with three lit incense sticks [4]. |
| **Bouyei people** | Offer rice cakes at the doorway to the "Moon Grandmother" [4]. |
| **Korean minority (Yanbian)** | A "moon house" of dry pine branches lets moonlight shine inside [4]. |

## 📖 The Moon in Poetry

Poets are a big reason the festival feels the way it does. The moon became shorthand for homesickness and reunion [36][40].

- **Su Shi (苏轼, 1037–1101),** *Prelude to Water Melody* (水调歌头·明月几时有). Written on the Mid-Autumn Festival of 1076 while thinking of his younger brother **Su Zhe (苏辙)** [36][49]. It opens by questioning the moon and the heavens, and it accepts that sorrow and joy, parting and reunion are natural, like the moon's waxing and waning [49][11]. The singer **Faye Wong** made a hit song, *"Wishing We Last Forever"*, from the poem [36]. *(Poem text not reproduced here; many licensed translations are available online.)*
- **Li Bai (李白),** *Quiet Night Thought* (静夜思). A four-line, five-character-per-line Tang poem of homesickness under the moon [54][40].
- **Others:** CGTN notes that poets such as Liu Yuxi also wrote about the moon and the festival, and that those poems have resonated with readers from ancient times to the present [36].

## 🏙️ Mid-Autumn in Modern Times

### 📅 The holiday today

- Made a statutory holiday from 1 January 2008, alongside Qingming and the Dragon Boat Festival, as part of the State Council's push to promote traditional culture [3][22].
- **2026:** Friday 25 September. The break runs 25–27 September, effectively one statutory day joined to the weekend, and it is **not** joined with National Day (1–7 October) this year [33][35].
- Urban life had reduced the festival's influence for a time, and it became more commercial. Baidu Baike says it has gradually regained prominence [22].

### 🎁 Gifting and mooncake culture

- **A pullback from extravagance:** During the 2010s anti-extravagance campaign, officials were discouraged from lavish gifts, and luxury mooncake sales fell sharply [30]. Younger people are more likely to buy a small box they will actually eat, bake their own, or choose snow-skin flavors [30].
- **Less packaging, less sugar:** Modern consumers favor low-sugar recipes, natural ingredients and sustainable design over showy packaging [11][32]. Hong Kong makers cut packaging under a voluntary agreement [4].
- **Museum collabs as status symbols:** Mooncakes made with institutions like the Palace Museum or Dunhuang Academy have become status items [11].
- **Nostalgia counter-trend:** A China Daily-reported trend has people seeking traditional recipes that recall childhood [31].
- **Gift boxes:** In Hong Kong, a four-mooncake box of lotus paste with yolks can cost about US$40 or more [4].

### 📱 New ways to celebrate

- **"Reverse reunions":** aging parents travel to megacities to visit working children, avoiding peak travel [11].
- **"Cloud reunions":** HD video calls let scattered families share the same moonlit hour [11].
- **Immersive culture:** young people wear *hanfu* to night markets, join dynasty-themed murder-mystery games in old towns, and even book "moon-viewing flights" [11]. On TV, extended reality has projected virtual Tang poets onto digital lunar landscapes [11].
- **Digital gifts:** Many people send WeChat red envelopes or use the holiday to travel [41].
- **Pop-culture crossovers:** In 2023 a *Black Myth: Wukong*-themed Mid-Autumn event was held at McDonald's in Shanghai [3], and Wuhan Polar Ocean Park staged an underwater performance of Chang'e flying to the moon [3].
- **Lanterns go electric:** Battery-powered lanterns and glow sticks have largely replaced candle-lit paper ones, prompting environmental appeals [26].

### 🚀 Chang'e in space

China's lunar program is named after the moon goddess. Chang'e-1 reached lunar orbit in 2007, Chang'e-3 (2013) and Chang'e-4 (2019) landed and roved, and Chang'e-5 (2020) and Chang'e-6 (2024) returned samples, the latter from the far side of the moon [39][38]. **Chang'e-7**, aimed at the lunar south pole, was about to launch in late August 2026, but on 23 August China announced it was postponing the mission, saying it "cannot take place during the planned window this year" [38]. As of the latest reports I found, it has not launched.

### 🌍 Beyond China

- Chinatown Mid-Autumn events are held across North America, in cities such as San Francisco, Chicago, Philadelphia and New York [4].
- In Singapore, Chinatown's celebration is famous for illuminated sculptures and street lanterns [48].

## ⚖️ Then vs. Now

| Aspect | 🏯 Traditionally | 🏙️ Today |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Moon rites** | Outdoor altar, incense, fruit and cake offerings, often led by women [46][4] | Rare in big cities, still seen in towns, villages and some southern regions [13][29] |
| **Mooncakes** | Homemade or shared among the household; cut into equal pieces [4] | Store-bought gift boxes, shifting to smaller, lower-sugar, creative and museum-branded versions [30][11] |
| **Lanterns** | Candle-lit paper lanterns in animal and flower shapes [13][26] | Battery/LED lanterns, giant city light shows [14][26] |
| **Family** | Everyone gathers under the same roof | Travel rush, "reverse reunions" and video "cloud reunions" [11] |
| **Entertainment** | Moon viewing, riddles, opera, dragon dances [13] | Hanfu night markets, murder-mystery games, XR galas, moon-viewing flights [11] |
| **Meaning** | Harvest thanks and moon worship [2] | Family reunion is the "primary cultural connotation" [22] |
| **Legal status** | Folk festival | National heritage (2006) and public holiday (2008) [22] |

## 🌏 Cousins Across Asia

The same full moon is celebrated in many places on the same date [4]:

- 🇰🇷 **Chuseok (추석):** a major three-day harvest holiday, focused on visiting hometowns and honoring ancestors [4].
- 🇯🇵 **Tsukimi (月見):** "moon viewing," with picnics and sake under the full moon [4], and dango offerings [55].
- 🇻🇳 **Tết Trung Thu:** the "Children's Festival," with lantern parades, lion dances and masks [4].
- 🇰🇭 🇱🇦 🇲🇲 🇱🇰 **Full-moon festivals** with Buddhist roots, like Cambodia's Bon Om Touk and Myanmar's Thadingyut [4].

## ⚠️ Notes on Conflicting Sources

Honest research means flagging where sources disagree:

1. **Where "Mid-Autumn" first appears.** Several sources say the *Rites of Zhou* [1][4][6], while another says the *Book of Rites* from the Han [2]. Either way, early on it named a *season*, not a festival.
2. **When the festival "began."** Some say the early Tang [5], others the Northern Song [1][2]. It developed gradually.
3. **The mooncake rebellion story** is popular folklore, not settled history [17][11].
4. **Origin of mooncakes.** The Tang stories credit different emperors (Taizong [4] or Gaozu [21]).
5. **Dragon length at Tai Hang:** about 67 m [15] versus "more than 70 m" [12] (and about 200 feet in Wikipedia [4]).
6. **Length of the holiday.** Some sources describe a 3-day holiday [33][35] and others a 1-day statutory holiday [41]. Both fit: there is one statutory day, attached to the weekend.
7. **Many sources here are travel and lifestyle sites.** They are useful for descriptions of customs, but for academic-level claims, seek scholarly works such as those cited in Wikipedia's reference list (for example Stepanchuk & Wong, *Mooncakes and Hungry Ghosts*, 1991; Yang Lemei, "China's Mid-Autumn Day," *Journal of Folklore Research*, 2006) [4].
8. **Poetry lines** are described rather than quoted in this guide.
